newsitem.title: USA: Gold prices dip to 3-year low, cocoa also falls.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices dip to 3-year low, cocoa also falls.

text.p: Gold prices continued to slide Wednesday, tumbling to the lowest levels seen in more than three years before staging a modest late rally.
"The bear market has clearly begun," said Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold, noting the prospect of further sales by central banks continued to weigh on the market.

"We have already seen 1,300 (metric) tons of gold sold by European central banks since the Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992 and we would be very surprised if this year did not bring sales of at least another 300 to 500 tons," he said.
Prices dipped early, with a morning fix in London of $343.15, the lowest since September 1993. It closed in New York at $343.90/344.40, down from a previous $344.00/344.50.
Dealers said producers in countries such as South Africa were becoming increasingly nervous about the price outlook and some may be looking to make forward sales.
COMEX April gold closed unchanged at $346.40 an ounce, but not before posting a new contract low of $344.30.

Cocoa prices on New York's Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange plunged for the second day in a row as speculators continued to sell heavily amid plentiful nearby supplies. The key March contract ended off $22 a metric ton at $1,272.
March cocoa has tumbled $51 -- or nearly 4 percent -- in two days despite a pair of estimates projecting a global supply deficit in the 1996/97 season.
"The market ignored news of a deficit," one trader said. "If you put out bullish news and a market does not react, it is very bearish."
Earlier this week the International Cocoa Organisation (ICCO) forecast a world cocoa deficit of 225,000 tons in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) compared with an estimated surplus of 133,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
The ICCO report came on the heels of an estimate by British trade house E.D.& F. Man, which forecast a supply deficit of between 170,000 and 230,000 tons in 1996/97.
But Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson said good stock availablity in the near-term has weighed on values.
"The deficit is a longer term statisical physical situation," Stevenson said. "In the short-term, supplies are ample and there is a lot of cocoa in the pipeline."
Heating oil extended its decline Wednesday after oil inventory data showed higher distillate output when heating oil supply was already deemed ample amid mild weather.

"The main feature of the day was weakness in the refined product contracts, with refinery runs up more than one percent when distributors are trying to destock heat," said Jim Ritterbusch, a dealer with Sweeney Oil in Illinois.

Heating oil for March delivery settled off 0.86 cent at 63.32 cents a gallon on the New York Mercantile Exchange after falling 1.10 cents Tuesday. March gasoline finished down 0.77 cent a gallon at 67.54 cents while March crude ended off 11 cents at $23.91 a barrel.

Crude's declines were limited by higher refinery operating rates. This translates into more crude being used when oil inventory data released by American Petroleum Institute (API) on Tuesday said crude stocks are 9.60 million barrels below a year ago for the week ended Jan. 31.
The API said that refinery capacity utilization rates rose 1.2 percentage points to 90.3 percent when traders had been expecting the rate to decline by 0.5 percentage point.

Consequently, output of distillate, which includes heating il and diesel, grew to 3.20 million from 3.10 million just when distillate stocks were showing a surplus with year ago levels for the first time since June 1995. Heating oil output grew to 1.40 million barrels from 1.37 million barrels.

Mild temperatures in the northeastern United States, the largest heating oil market in the world, is tempering heat demand, dealers said. Independent forecaster Weather Services Corp expected temperatures to average normal to above normal through the weekend in the Northeast.
